title: Six Things to Know About BNEF’s New US Data Center Capacity Outlook | BloombergNEF
gist: BloombergNEF lifted its US data center capacity forecast to 118GW by 2030 (+52% vs December 2025) and 194GW by 2035 (+83%), with non-hyperscalers and first-time developers driving most of the new pipeline. Energy access, not chips, is the binding constraint: an AI-chip-implied buildout would need 63GW more US capacity by 2033 than BNEF thinks gets built, and 48GW of on-site gas must be constructed by 2035 unless grid interconnection accelerates past its ~10GW-per-year record.

insights.claim: BloombergNEF's forecast for installed US data center capacity in 2030 is now 118GW, a 52% upward revision from its December 2025 forecast.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: A 52% revision in seven months means capital-spend and power-demand models built on 2025 vintage forecasts are materially too low; re-underwrite anything sized off them.
insights.quote: BloombergNEF’s forecasted 2030 installed US data center capacity is now 118 gigawatts (GW), an upwards revision of 52% compared to our December 2025 forecast.
insights.locator: 1. Our forecast has gone up again.

insights.claim: The 2035 US data center capacity forecast was raised to 194GW, an 83% upward revision, so the revision is larger the further out the horizon goes.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Uncertainty compounds with tenor: long-dated power, land and equipment assumptions carry far more revision risk than near-term ones.
insights.quote: We expect 194GW of data centers to be online in the US by 2035 – an 83% upward revision.
insights.locator: We expect 194GW of data centers

insights.claim: The single biggest driver of the upward revision is that the announced US data center pipeline grew by a further 101GW since December 2025, pulling more capacity into the pre-2030 window.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Announcement flow is the leading indicator feeding these forecasts, so tracking monthly announced-GW is the cheapest way to anticipate the next revision.
insights.locator: There are a number of reasons

insights.claim: Nearly all public forecasts of US data center capacity have been revised upward over the past year, which BNEF reads as evidence of genuine uncertainty rather than confirmation, alongside a rising share of projects that are 'gigascale'.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Consensus moving in one direction is not the same as consensus being right; size positions for a wide distribution of buildout outcomes, not a point estimate.
insights.quote: Most public forecasts of US data center capacity have also been revised up in the past year, underlining the level of uncertainty around how much capacity will get built
insights.locator: Most public forecasts of US data center capacity

themes.theme: AI Chip Scenario as Upper Bound

insights.claim: For the first time BNEF built a second scenario off Bloomberg Intelligence's AI chip sales outlook, implying as much as 325GW of data center power capacity added globally between 2023 and 2033 if nothing else constrained the build.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Chip shipments now function as a demand-side ceiling for power infrastructure; semis order books become a forward indicator for grid and generation equipment demand.
insights.locator: 2. We’ve integrated an AI chip scenario

insights.claim: Of the 325GW of globally chip-implied data center power capacity to 2033, BNEF expects 207GW to land in the US.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Roughly two-thirds of chip-driven power demand is a US siting problem, concentrating the equipment, gas and interconnection opportunity domestically.
insights.locator: BNEF’s AI chip scenario indicates

insights.claim: There is a 63GW gap between the US capacity AI chip shipments imply should be built by 2033 and what BNEF forecasts will actually be built, and the cause is energy constraints rather than demand.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Electricity supply, not compute appetite, is the throttle on AI buildout; scarcity value accrues to whoever controls power, interconnection queue position and on-site generation.
insights.quote: This means there is a 63GW gap in capacity between what AI chip shipments imply should get built in the US by 2033, and what BNEF’s data center forecast says will actually get built, due to energy constraints.
insights.locator: This means there is a 63GW gap

insights.claim: The true capacity shortfall is larger than 63GW because the AI-chip scenario only models demand from AI servers and ignores all non-AI data center workloads.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Headline AI-power gap numbers understate total power tightness, which supports a longer runway for power-adjacent assets than AI-only framing suggests.
insights.quote: The real shortfall is larger, as the AI-chip scenario only models demand from AI servers.
insights.locator: The real shortfall is larger

insights.claim: BNEF lays out four mutually exclusive resolutions to the chip-versus-capacity gap: faster chip replacement cycles, more chips deployed outside the US, fewer chips ultimately purchased than modelled, or data centers and power capacity built at unprecedented rates.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: This is a clean decision tree: each branch has a different trade — shorter refresh favors semis, offshoring favors non-US power markets, fewer chips is the bear case for the whole complex.
insights.locator: There are a few factors that could close this gap

insights.claim: BNEF split its forecast by developer type for the first time, and non-hyperscaler capacity nearly quintuples over the next decade versus a tripling for hyperscalers.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: The marginal buyer of turbines, transformers and land is increasingly not a Microsoft-grade balance sheet, which changes credit quality and counterparty risk across the supply chain.
insights.locator: 3. We have split out developer type

insights.claim: By 2035 hyperscaler data center capacity reaches 57GW against 138GW for non-hyperscalers, so roughly 70% of US capacity sits outside the four largest cloud operators.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Sizing exposure to the AI buildout purely through mega-cap capex misses the majority of the physical build.
insights.quote: By 2035, hyperscaler capacity reaches 57GW, compared with 138GW for non-hyperscalers.
insights.locator: By 2035, hyperscaler capacity reaches 57GW

insights.claim: Although Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet and Amazon Web Services have faster development timelines, most new capacity entering the project pipeline is from non-hyperscalers, driven by an increasing number of giga-campuses.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Speed and volume have decoupled: the fastest builders are no longer the biggest source of new pipeline, so pipeline-weighted forecasts should be discounted for slower delivery.
insights.locator: While hyperscalers – specifically Microsoft, Meta

insights.claim: BNEF expects AI training and inference to account for more than half of total US data center capacity, with colocation the next largest workload category.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Majority-AI workload mix means data center load shapes get less predictable, raising the value of firm, flexible on-site power and storage.
insights.quote: BNEF expects AI training and inference to account for more than half of total US data center capacity, followed by colocation.
insights.locator: Data center market share by workload

insights.claim: Workload and operator mix determines both siting strategy and energy consumption because different workloads carry different utilization profiles.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Utilization profile, not nameplate GW, drives actual MWh demand — use it to sanity-check utility load forecasts and PPA pricing.
insights.locator: Data center market share by workload and operator type

insights.claim: Of the 100 largest announced US data center projects, 52 were announced by companies that have never built a data center before, accounting for 87GW of capacity.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: A majority of the largest projects sit with unproven sponsors — a direct argument for haircutting announced pipelines and for scrutinizing offtake counterparties.
insights.quote: We found that 52 of the largest 100 projects in the US are announced by companies that have never built one before, accounting for 87GW.
insights.locator: 4. We recognize there is a new developer risk

insights.claim: BNEF explicitly declines to call inexperienced sponsorship a cancellation signal, framing it instead as elevated execution risk.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: The expected failure mode is delay and cost overrun rather than outright cancellation, which favors suppliers paid on progress over those paid on completion.
insights.quote: This may not lead to cancellations but it increases execution risk.
insights.locator: This may not lead to cancellations

insights.claim: The median developer scaling factor for the 100 largest projects — the ratio of a project to the largest project that developer previously delivered — rose from 2.1 in 1Q 2015 to 8.7 in 4Q 2025.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Even experienced developers are attempting projects roughly nine times their largest prior delivery; this single ratio is the cleanest quantitative screen for delivery risk in the sector.
insights.quote: the median developer scaling factor – the ratio between a given project and the largest project previously delivered by its developer – rose from 2.1 in 1Q 2015 to 8.7 in 4Q 2025
insights.locator: For the 100 largest projects

insights.claim: BNEF's revision work rested on digging into the details of the 150 largest announced US projects to isolate developer type and regional considerations.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: The forecast is bottom-up and project-level, so it will move with individual mega-project news rather than smoothly.
insights.locator: This time around BNEF dug into the details

insights.claim: Hyperscalers now take 5.3 years from preconstruction through construction, versus 8.4 years for non-hyperscalers — a three-year delivery penalty for the group building most of the new pipeline.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Capacity announced today by non-hyperscalers largely lands in the mid-2030s, pushing out the equipment revenue curve versus headline announcement dates.
insights.quote: Hyperscalers are now taking 5.3 years for development, compared to non-hyperscalers taking 8.4 years.
insights.locator: 5. Development timelines are shortening

insights.claim: The timeline gap is concentrated in preconstruction — 3 years for hyperscalers against 5.7 years for non-hyperscalers — implying operator identity matters most before ground is broken and that execution risk historically narrows once construction starts.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Construction start is the de-risking milestone worth trading around; pre-construction announcements deserve heavy probability discounts regardless of sponsor.
insights.quote: The gap is most stark in the preconstruction phase (3 years versus 5.7 years), implying that operator type matters most before a project breaks ground
insights.locator: The gap is most stark in the preconstruction phase

insights.claim: BNEF flags West Texas as a key market where execution risk may be rising even after construction begins, cutting against the general rule that risk falls once a project breaks ground.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Concentration in West Texas is now a specific regional risk to monitor rather than a diversification benefit for anyone with exposure there.
insights.quote: Although BNEF is monitoring key markets such as West Texas where execution risk may be rising.
insights.locator: Although BNEF is monitoring key markets

themes.theme: On-Site Gas as the Binding Constraint

insights.claim: There is 124GW of announced on-site gas plant capacity being built for US data centers, but BNEF has mapped only 56% of it to a target commissioning date.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Roughly half of announced on-site gas has no schedule attached, so gas turbine and engine order books will convert from announcements far more slowly than the headline GW implies.
insights.locator: 6. On-site gas generation must play a significant role

insights.claim: The most new data center demand the US power grid has ever connected in a single year is estimated at just 10GW, setting a hard reference ceiling on grid-led growth.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Compare any buildout forecast against this 10GW-per-year historical record to test plausibility; anything far above it requires behind-the-meter generation.
insights.quote: The most new data center demand that the US power grid has connected in one year is estimated by BNEF as 10GW.
insights.locator: The most new data center demand

insights.claim: If the grid's connection rate does not accelerate beyond its historical pace, 48GW of on-site gas generation must be built by 2035 just to hit BNEF's base-case data center forecast.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: That is a quantified floor of demand for turbines, reciprocating engines and gas supply over the next decade, largely independent of how the AI upside scenario resolves.
insights.quote: If this rate does not accelerate, 48GW of on-site gas needs to be built by 2035 to meet BNEF’s base-case data center forecast.
insights.locator: If this rate does not accelerate

insights.claim: BNEF does not believe enough credible on-site gas capacity has been announced to meet the AI-chip scenario unless the grid's ability to connect new data centers rises significantly.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: The bullish AI-chip case is not financeable on current gas announcements alone; interconnection reform is the swing variable for the upside scenario.
insights.quote: BNEF does not believe there is enough credible on-site gas capacity announced to meet the AI-chip scenario without a significant increase in the grid’s ability to connect new data centers.
insights.locator: BNEF does not believe there is enough credible

insights.claim: A further 50GW of speculative on-site gas projects have been announced with no associated timeline, which BNEF treats as headroom that could let the AI-chip scenario be met by data center build.
insights.speaker: BloombergNEF (free content)
insights.so_what: Watch for these timeline-less projects acquiring commissioning dates — that conversion is the earliest observable signal that the upside scenario is becoming real.
insights.locator: There are however 50GW of speculative on-site gas projects
